request.prompt:
You are clustering code review findings from the same PR. For each PAIR below, decide whether the two findings describe the SAME underlying issue — same root cause in the same code location. Different wording is fine. A finding about a DIFFERENT defect in the same file or function is NOT the same issue. Severity or aspect differences of the same root cause ARE the same issue.


For THIS scoring pass, duplicate equivalence is stricter than sharing a root cause.
You must compare the COMPLETE MATERIAL CLAIMS, including mechanism, triggering
conditions, execution path, and consequence. The same line or broad concern does
not establish equivalence. A report of wrong-category selection, a case/rename
mismatch, a crash, and a silent fallback are different claims even at one lookup.
An inactive/unbound API concern and an alleged active user-facing failure differ.
A compound report with an additional material claim does NOT equal its subset.
Differences only in wording, severity, or hedging do not create separate claims.
If the claimed mechanisms, triggers or consequences conflict, or one report adds
an unsupported/different material factual claim, return same=false. You are NOT
verifying which claim is true; do not repair or reinterpret either report to make
them match. If unsure whether their full claims are equivalent, return false.

For every numbered pair, extract what A and B actually CLAIM into mechanism,
trigger and consequence. Then list material_differences and give your equivalence
verdict, confidence and reason. same=true requires no material differences.
Return ONLY this JSON object, with EVERY pair index exactly once:
{"pairs":[{"pair":1,"a":{"mechanism":"...","trigger":"...","consequence":"..."},"b":{"mechanism":"...","trigger":"...","consequence":"..."},"material_differences":[],"same":true,"confidence":0.9,"reason":"..."}]}

PAIR 18:
A: The booking create persists only `evt.destinationCalendar[0]` via the singular `connect`, so the additional collective team calendars exist only in-memory during creation and are never linked to the booking record. Downstream flows that rebuild CalendarEvent from the booking (reschedule, cancel, payment webhooks, bookingReminder) reconstruct at most the organizer's calendar, so the multi-calendar state this PR introduces is not durable and later operations touch only the first destination — the next change to cancellation/reschedule logic has to re-derive the member calendars independently.
B: The booking record connects only `evt.destinationCalendar[0]` even when the diff's new collective flow populates several destination calendars and creates calendar events for all of them. For collective bookings, the persisted Booking.destinationCalendar relation under-represents the actual destinations (only the organizer/eventType's is linked); any consumer that reconstructs evt from booking.destinationCalendar — the pattern this diff itself repeats in bookingReminder, payment webhooks, confirm/editLocation/requestReschedule handlers — sees only the first calendar, so future flows built on that relation will operate on one member's calendar while events exist on several.

Downstream flows that rebuild CalendarEvent from the booking (reschedule, cancel, payment webhooks, bookingReminder) reconstruct at most the organizer's calendar, so the multi-calendar state this PR introduces is not durable and later operations touch only the first destination — the next change to cancellation/reschedule logic has to re-derive the member calendars independently.
B: The booking record still connects only `evt.destinationCalendar[0]`, so the multi-host destination calendar list this PR introduces has no durable representation anywhere in the data model. Every post-creation flow (reschedule, cancel, reminders, payment webhooks) rebuilds destinationCalendar as a single-element array from booking.destinationCalendar, so the collective multi-host state exists only in memory during the initial create and cannot be audited or recovered from the booking afterwards.

PAIR 20:
A: The booking create persists only `evt.destinationCalendar[0]` via the singular `connect`, so the additional collective team calendars exist only in-memory during creation and are never linked to the booking record. Downstream flows that rebuild CalendarEvent from the booking (reschedule, cancel, payment webhooks, bookingReminder) reconstruct at most the organizer's calendar, so the multi-calendar state this PR introduces is not durable and later operations touch only the first destination — the next change to cancellation/reschedule logic has to re-derive the member calendars independently.
B: The Booking write still connects only `evt.destinationCalendar[0]` because the schema keeps a single one-to-one Booking→DestinationCalendar relation, so the multi-calendar model exists only in the in-memory CalendarEvent and is not persisted as the source of truth. Every later flow that rebuilds the CalendarEvent from `booking.destinationCalendar` (confirm.handler, editLocation, paypal/stripe webhooks, bookingReminder cron — all wrapped as `[booking.destinationCalendar]` in this diff) sees only the first host's calendar; the collective multi-host state is unrepresentable in the data model and is silently lost after creation.
